claim: Multidomain proteins occur predominately in all three kingdoms of life.
source: However, it is widely recognized that throughout all three kingdoms of life, proteins occur predominately in multidomain forms (Apic et al., 2001; Ekman et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to Apic et al., 2001 and Ekman et al., 2005

claim: Multidomain proteins consist of more than one structural building unit, or domain.
source: As their name indicates, multidomain proteins consist of more than one structural building unit, or domain (Teichmann et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citation to Teichmann et al., 1999

claim: Domains themselves have a strong tendency to fold.
source: Domains themselves have a strong tendency to fold (Murzin et al., 1995)
evidence: Supported by citation to Murzin et al., 1995

claim: The folding of a multidomain protein usually takes a more complex form than a simple sum of folding of individual domains.
source: but although there is high structural modularity in a multidomain protein (Han et al., 2007), the folding of a multidomain protein usually takes a more complex form than a simple sum of folding of individual domains (Levy, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Han et al., 2007 and Levy, 2017

claim: Domain interfaces or linkers play nonuniversal roles in modulating folding stability.
source: The key component in the folding of a multidomain protein is the interaction of domain interfaces or linkers, which have been found to play nonuniversal roles in modulating folding stability (Fast et al., 2009; Bhaskara et al., 2013; Vishwanath et al., 2018)
evidence: Supported by citations to Fast et al., 2009; Bhaskara et al., 2013; Vishwanath et al., 2018

claim: Domain interfaces or linkers play nonuniversal roles in modulating folding cooperativity.
source: The key component in the folding of a multidomain protein is the interaction of domain interfaces or linkers, which have been found to play nonuniversal roles in modulating folding stability (Fast et al., 2009; Bhaskara et al., 2013; Vishwanath et al., 2018), cooperativity (Batey et al., 2005)
evidence: Supported by citation to Batey et al., 2005

claim: Domain interfaces or linkers play nonuniversal roles in modulating folding kinetics.
source: The key component in the folding of a multidomain protein is the interaction of domain interfaces or linkers, which have been found to play nonuniversal roles in modulating folding stability (Fast et al., 2009; Bhaskara et al., 2013; Vishwanath et al., 2018), cooperativity (Batey et al., 2005) and kinetics (Osváth et al., 2005; Batey et al., 2006; Batey and Clarke, 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to Osváth et al., 2005; Batey et al., 2006; Batey and Clarke, 2006

claim: Efficient folding of a multidomain protein is vital for providing structural scaffolds for biological function.
source: Efficient folding of a multidomain protein is vital not only for providing structural scaffolds for biological function (Vogel et al., 2004)
evidence: Supported by citation to Vogel et al., 2004

claim: Efficient folding of a multidomain protein is vital for preventing misfolding.
source: Efficient folding of a multidomain protein is vital not only for providing structural scaffolds for biological function (Vogel et al., 2004), but also for preventing misfolding (Strucksberg et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Strucksberg et al., 2007

claim: Multidomain proteins are more prone to aggregation during folding processes than single-domain proteins.
source: Multidomain proteins, which often possess significant domain interfaces, are more prone to aggregation during folding processes than single-domain proteins (Han et al., 2007; Borgia et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Han et al., 2007 and Borgia et al., 2011

claim: In vivo, multidomain proteins can undergo co-translational folding.
source: It has been suggested that in vivo, multidomain proteins can undergo co-translational folding (Fedorov and Baldwin, 1997)
evidence: Supported by citation to Fedorov and Baldwin, 1997

claim: In co-translational folding, each domain folds sequentially one-by-one during protein synthesis from the ribosome.
source: It has been suggested that in vivo, multidomain proteins can undergo co-translational folding (Fedorov and Baldwin, 1997), where each domain folds sequentially one-by-one during protein synthesis from the ribosome (Netzer and Hartl, 1997; Frydman et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citations to Netzer and Hartl, 1997 and Frydman et al., 1999

claim: A 'divide-and-conquer' scenario has been proposed for in vitro multidomain protein folding.
source: Likewise, a 'divide-and-conquer' scenario has been proposed for in vitro multidomain protein folding, where all domains fold independently, followed by coalescence of neighbors (Wang et al., 2012a).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wang et al., 2012a

claim: The reactive center loop (RCL) plays a critical role in the folding of serpin to distinct structures.
source: A recent computational study of a two-domain serpin elucidated the critical role of the functional binding-related reactive center loop (RCL) in the folding of the protein to distinct structures (Giri Rao and Gosavi, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Giri Rao and Gosavi, 2018

claim: Folding of serpin to the metastable active structure is faster than folding to the stable latent structure.
source: Folding of the serpin to the metastable active structure, where the RCL is present as an intradomain segment, is faster than folding to the stable latent structure, where the RCL is involved in extensive interactions between domains.
evidence: Supported by citation to Giri Rao and Gosavi, 2018 in the preceding sentence

claim: Removal of interdomain interactions had little effect on the folding cooperativity of a three-domain adenylate kinase.
source: Other work using a similar model, however, indicated that removal of interdomain interactions had little effect on the folding cooperativity of a three-domain adenylate kinase (Giri Rao and Gosavi, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Giri Rao and Gosavi, 2014

claim: Domain connectivity and interactions in multidomain proteins determine folding pathways, cooperativity, and kinetics.
source: Using statistical mechanical models, Sasai and co-workers investigated a variety of multidomain proteins and their circular permutants. Their results showed that domain connectivity and interactions in multidomain proteins determine folding pathways, cooperativity, and kinetics (Itoh and Sasai, 2008; Inanami et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Itoh and Sasai, 2008 and Inanami et al., 2014

claim: Interdomain interactions are fundamental for generating and stabilizing the correct multidomain folds.
source: From a structural perspective, the effects of neighboring domains in terms of interdomain interactions are fundamental for generating and stabilizing the correct multidomain folds (Jones et al., 2000; Bhaskara and Srinivasan, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Jones et al., 2000 and Bhaskara and Srinivasan, 2011

claim: Relatively weak interdomain interactions trigger domain motions in multidomain proteins, making a pivotal contribution to protein function.
source: Usually, the relatively weak interdomain interactions trigger domain motions in multidomain proteins, making a pivotal contribution to protein function (Bennett and Huber, 1984; Schulz, 1991; Miyashita et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bennett and Huber, 1984; Schulz, 1991; Miyashita et al., 2003

claim: Native folds of proteins may exhibit a certain degree of frustration in favor of functional state switching.
source: As is now widely recognized, the native folds of proteins may exhibit a certain degree of frustration in favor of functional state switching (Ferreiro et al., 2007; Ferreiro et al., 2014; Whitford and Onuchic, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ferreiro et al., 2007; Ferreiro et al., 2014; Whitford and Onuchic, 2015

claim: DPO4 consists of a polymerase core with finger, palm, and thumb domains, as well as a little figure domain connected to the polymerase core by a flexible linker.
source: Akin to the other Y-family polymerases, DPO4 consists of a polymerase core with a right-handed architecture, including finger (F), palm (P), and thumb (T) domains, as well as a little figure (LF) domain that is connected to the polymerase core by a flexible linker (Figure 1A; Ling et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ling et al., 2001 and reference to Figure 1A

claim: Many more intradomain contacts than interdomain contacts are present in the apo form of DPO4.
source: Structural analysis has shown that many more intradomain contacts than interdomain contacts are present in the apo form of DPO4 (Wong et al., 2008; Appendix 2—table 1).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wong et al., 2008 and reference to Appendix 2—table 1

claim: Thermal unfolding experiments have indicated the existence of one intermediate state in DPO4.
source: Thermal unfolding experiments have indicated the existence of one intermediate state (Sherrer et al., 2012)
evidence: Supported by citation to Sherrer et al., 2012

claim: The intermediate state in DPO4 is probably formed by the unfolding of the linker interactions with the domains.
source: Thermal unfolding experiments have indicated the existence of one intermediate state (Sherrer et al., 2012), which is probably formed by the unfolding of the linker interactions with the domains.
evidence: Based on inference from thermal unfolding experiments

claim: Binding of DPO4 to DNA is an essential step in nucleotide incorporation.
source: Binding of DPO4 to DNA is an essential step in nucleotide incorporation (Fiala and Suo, 2004; Wong et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Fiala and Suo, 2004 and Wong et al., 2008

claim: Significant rotation and translation of the LF domain occur during DNA binding, while the domain structures remain unchanged.
source: Structural comparisons of DPO4 in apo form and DNA binary form have revealed that significant rotation and translation of the LF domain occur during DNA binding, while the domain structures remain unchanged (Wong et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wong et al., 2008

claim: The 'open-to-closed' conformational transition in DPO4 is pivotal to the formation of a high-affinity DPO4–DNA complex prior to nucleotide binding and incorporation.
source: This 'open-to-closed' conformational transition in DPO4 is pivotal to the formation of a high-affinity DPO4–DNA complex prior to nucleotide binding and incorporation (Fiala and Suo, 2004; Sherrer et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Fiala and Suo, 2004 and Sherrer et al., 2009

claim: The linker plays an important role in the conformational transition of DPO4.
source: Previous experimental and simulation studies have suggested that the linker plays an important role in this conformational transition (Xing et al., 2009; Sherrer et al., 2012; Chu et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Xing et al., 2009; Sherrer et al., 2012; Chu et al., 2014

claim: The 2D free energy landscape reveals a complex DPO4 folding process with multiple intermediate states.
source: The 2D free energy landscape reveals a complex DPO4 folding process with multiple intermediate states.
evidence: Based on data from simulations shown in Figure 1A

claim: The existence of intermediate states in DPO4 folding is in good agreement with the results of temperature-induced unfolding experiments.
source: The existence of these intermediate states in DPO4 folding is in good agreement with the results of temperature-induced unfolding experiments, which revealed more than one transition during the unfolding of DPO4 (Sherrer et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sherrer et al., 2012 and comparison with simulation data

claim: DPO4 folding complies with a 'divide-and-conquer' framework.
source: Overall, DPO4 folding complies with a 'divide-and-conquer' framework (Wang et al., 2012a).
evidence: Based on structural analysis from simulations and supported by citation to Wang et al., 2012a

claim: Backtracking is most probable when the interdomain interaction strength is higher than the default value in the SBM.
source: Further analysis of the number of backtracking shows that backtracking is most probable when the interdomain interaction strength is higher than the default value in the SBM (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Based on data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4

claim: Backtracking in DPO4 folding is led by unstable and fast domain folding and unfolding of the small-sized F and T domains.
source: Therefore, we suggest that the backtracking in DPO4 folding is led by unstable and fast domain folding and unfolding of the small-sized F and T domains (Figure 2—figure supplement 5).
evidence: Based on structural analysis from simulations shown in Figure 2E and F

claim: There is high cooperative folding in the DPO4 core.
source: In Figure 2G, we can see that there is high cooperative folding in the DPO4 core.
evidence: Based on TCI data shown in Figure 2G

claim: The conserved DPO4 core is a stable structural unit that unfolds cooperatively.
source: This is consistent with the experimental evidence that the conserved DPO4 core is a stable structural unit that unfolds cooperatively (Sherrer et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sherrer et al., 2012

claim: When the interdomain interaction is weakened, DPO4 folding cooperativity decreases.
source: When the interdomain interaction is weakened, DPO4 folding cooperativity decreases (Figure 2H).
evidence: Based on data shown in Figure 2H

claim: A moderate increase in interdomain interaction strength can significantly increase the folding cooperativity of DPO4 for values of ρ in the range 0.5–1.0.
source: Overall, we find that a moderate increase in interdomain interaction strength can significantly increase the folding cooperativity of DPO4 (for values of ρ in the range 0.5–1.0).
evidence: Based on analysis of MTCI data from Figure 2H

claim: Weakening interdomain interactions promotes domain folding.
source: Intuitively, weakening interdomain interactions (decreasing ρ) should promote domain folding (Figure 3B)
evidence: Based on kinetic data shown in Figure 3B

claim: When interdomain interactions are weak (ρ in the range 0.5–0.9), the formation of interfaces between domains in DPO4 consumes more time than domain folding and thus is the rate-limiting step.
source: When interdomain interactions are weak (ρ in the range 0.5–0.9), the formation of interfaces between domains in DPO4 consumes more time than domain folding and thus is the rate-limiting step.
evidence: Based on analysis of kinetic data from Figure 3A and B

claim: When ρ is high (≥1.0), domain folding is slow and may become the rate-limiting step.
source: When ρ is high (≥1.0), corresponding to the case of weak intradomain interactions, domain folding is slow and may become the rate-limiting step (Figure 3B).
evidence: Based on analysis of kinetic data from Figure 3B

claim: The formation of the T–LF interface and the linker are significantly accelerated when ρ increases from 0.5 to 0.8.
source: The formation of the T–LF interface and the linker are significantly accelerated when ρ increases from 0.5 to 0.8.
evidence: Based on kinetic data from Figure 3C

claim: The T–LF interface and the linker are critical to DPO4–DNA functional binding.
source: These two interdomain structures are critical to DPO4–DNA functional binding, where a large-scale 'open-to-closed' conformational transition with rearrangement of the T–LF interface and the linker has been observed between apo-DPO4 and DNA-binding DPO4 (Wong et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wong et al., 2008

claim: There is an increase in binding affinity with strengthening interdomain interactions.
source: We find an increase in binding affinity with strengthening interdomain interactions (increasing ρ)
evidence: Based on free energy landscape data from umbrella sampling simulations shown in Figure 4A

claim: A multistate DPO4–DNA binding process is observed for all ρ.
source: For all ρ, we observe a similar multistate DPO4–DNA binding process, which we divide into four binding states (Figure 4B)
evidence: Based on free energy landscape data shown in Figure 4A and B

claim: The stabilities of both the BS and IS compared with the US are enhanced by increasing the strength of the interdomain interactions.
source: The stabilities of both the BS and IS compared with the US are enhanced by increasing the strength of the interdomain interactions, as evidenced by the free energy landscapes.
evidence: Based on analysis of free energy landscape data

claim: During binding, DPO4 itself can have three different forms: apo-DPO4, DNA binary DPO4, and intermediate DPO4.
source: Besides, we find that during binding, DPO4 itself can have three different forms: apo-DPO4, DNA binary DPO4, and intermediate DPO4 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Based on conformational distribution data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claim: Increasing ρ leads to a higher population of the apo form in the IS.
source: In the IS, DPO4 can interconvert between the apo and intermediate forms. Increasing ρ leads to a higher population of the apo form (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Based on conformational distribution data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claim: In the BS, DPO4 is in binary form, although large conformational fluctuations can be observed.
source: In the BS, DPO4 is in binary form, although large conformational fluctuations can be observed (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Based on conformational distribution data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claim: The structural fluctuations of DPO4 have little effect on the diffusion coefficient D.
source: Although for low ρ, DPO4 exhibits excessive conformational flexibility (Figure 4—figure supplement 3), which is assumed to increase the hydrodynamic radius of the chain (Huang and Liu, 2009), we find little effect of the structural fluctuations on D.
evidence: Based on diffusion coefficient data shown in Figure 4C and structural fluctuation data in Figure 4—figure supplement 3

claim: The capture rate of DNA by DPO4 in the first step of the binding process should be similar for different interaction strengths of DPO4.
source: Our results indicate that the free spatial diffusion of a folded large multidomain protein is barely affected by interfacial domain formation. Therefore, the capture rate of DNA by DPO4 in the first step of the binding process should be similar for different interaction strengths of DPO4, leading to ρ-independent observations.
evidence: Based on inference from diffusion coefficient data

claim: The weakly formed and flexible domain interface of DPO4 facilitates the DNA-binding process.
source: This indicates that the weakly formed and flexible domain interface of DPO4 facilitates the DNA-binding process.
evidence: Based on inference from encounter time data

claim: There is a strong correlation between the degree of conformational fluctuation of DPO4 and DNA-binding encounter times.
source: We further find a strong correlation between the degree of conformational fluctuation of DPO4, quantified by the root-mean-square fluctuation RMSF, and DNA-binding encounter times.
evidence: Based on correlation analysis shown in Figure 4D insert

claim: The transition times calculated from the metadynamics simulations are strongly correlated with the barrier heights measured by the umbrella sampling simulations for the transitions between the IS and the BS.
source: We find that the transition times calculated from the metadynamics simulations are strongly correlated with the barrier heights measured by the umbrella sampling simulations for the transitions between the IS and the BS (Figure 4—figure supplements 4 and 5).
evidence: Based on comparison of kinetic and thermodynamic data shown in Figure 4—figure supplements 4 and 5

claim: There is a monotonic increase in the kinetic times for both of the transitions between the IS and the BS as ρ increases.
source: We find a monotonic increase in the kinetic times for both of the transitions between the IS and the BS as ρ increases (Figure 4E).
evidence: Based on transition time data shown in Figure 4E

claim: Significant deceleration of the transition from the IS to the BS is found as the interdomain interactions in DPO4 become stronger.
source: In particular, significant deceleration of the transition from the IS to the BS is found as the interdomain interactions in DPO4 become stronger.
evidence: Based on transition time data shown in Figure 4E

claim: To achieve and maintain the conformation that underpins its biological function, DPO4 has to avoid strong interdomain interactions.
source: Although there are quantitative discrepancies between the thermodynamic and kinetic results (Figure 4—figure supplement 5), our results lead to the conclusion that to achieve and maintain the conformation that underpins its biological function, DPO4 has to avoid strong interdomain interactions, even when they are purely native.
evidence: Based on inference from thermodynamic and kinetic data

claim: Unfolding of truncated DPO4 mutants proceeds via cooperative processes.
source: Thermal denaturation experiments revealed that unfolding of truncated DPO4 mutants, such as the DPO4 core and LF domains, proceeds via cooperative processes (Sherrer et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sherrer et al., 2009

claim: Stopped-flow FRET studies revealed weak and strong interactions between and within each domain of DPO4, respectively.
source: Stopped-flow Förster resonance energy transfer (FRET) studies monitoring intradomain (Raper and Suo, 2016) and interdomain (Xu et al., 2009; Maxwell et al., 2014) conformational dynamics of DPO4 during DNA binding as well as nucleotide binding and incorporation revealed weak and strong interactions between and within each domain of DPO4, respectively.
evidence: Supported by citations to Raper and Suo, 2016; Xu et al., 2009; Maxwell et al., 2014

claim: An SBM with homogeneously weighted native contacts predicted a 'divide-and-conquer' domain-wise folding scenario for DPO4 folding.
source: Using only topological information, an SBM with homogeneously weighted native contacts predicted a 'divide-and-conquer' domain-wise folding scenario for DPO4 folding (Wang et al., 2012a; Chu et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Wang et al., 2012a and Chu et al., 2020

claim: Many multidomain proteins have stable domains that can fold independently.
source: Previous studies showed that many multidomain proteins have stable domains that can fold independently (Scott et al., 2002; Steward et al., 2002; Robertsson et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to Scott et al., 2002; Steward et al., 2002; Robertsson et al., 2005

claim: Proteins with independently folding domains exhibit a lack of densely packed domain interfaces.
source: From a structural perspective, these proteins exhibit a lack of densely packed domain interfaces, so their interdomain interactions should be minimal (Han et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Han et al., 2007

claim: Many proteins with independently folding domains are found not to fold in a 'sum of the parts' manner.
source: Nevertheless, the relatively weak interdomain interactions may still play an important role in the multidomain protein folding process, since many proteins with independently folding domains are found not to fold in a 'sum of the parts' manner (Levy, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Levy, 2017

claim: In the presence of weak interdomain interactions, the stability of the on-pathway folding intermediate states is enhanced.
source: In the presence of weak interdomain interactions, the stability of the on-pathway folding intermediate states is enhanced.
evidence: Based on thermodynamic data from Figure 1C

claim: Enhanced stability of intermediate states can promote a deterministic folding order of the domains in DPO4 to help eliminate backtracking.
source: This can promote a deterministic folding order of the domains in DPO4 to help eliminate backtracking, which usually acts as a kinetic trap during folding (Capraro et al., 2008; Gosavi et al., 2008).
evidence: Based on inference from simulation data and supported by citations to Capraro et al., 2008 and Gosavi et al., 2008

claim: If interdomain interactions are very weak, the folded states are destabilized, resulting in failed DPO4 folding.
source: However, if interdomain interactions are very weak, the folded states are destabilized, resulting in failed DPO4 folding.
evidence: Based on inference from thermodynamic data

claim: Strong interdomain interactions tend to couple domain folding and interface formation to fold the DPO4 as a whole.
source: By contrast, strong interdomain interactions tend to couple domain folding and interface formation to fold the DPO4 as a whole.
evidence: Based on inference from cooperativity and folding order data

claim: The 'all-or-none' DPO4 folding shows high cooperativity that disfavors the formation of intermediate states.
source: The 'all-or-none' DPO4 folding shows high cooperativity that disfavors the formation of intermediate states, so the folding order of DPO4 domains is not clearly defined.
evidence: Based on inference from cooperativity and folding order data

claim: The domains in DPO4 in the presence of strong interdomain interactions are destabilized by the relatively weak intradomain interactions, which induces more backtracking.
source: Besides, the domains in DPO4 in the presence of strong interdomain interactions are destabilized by the relatively weak intradomain interactions, which induces more backtracking.
evidence: Based on inference from backtracking data

claim: The fast folding of DPO4 requires weak interdomain interactions, so that DPO4 can efficiently use the 'divide-and-conquer' strategy to fold via modest cooperativity and limited backtracking.
source: Collectively, the fast folding of DPO4 requires weak interdomain interactions, so that DPO4 can efficiently use the 'divide-and-conquer' strategy to fold via modest cooperativity and limited backtracking.
evidence: Based on synthesis of folding kinetics, cooperativity, and backtracking data

claim: Weak interdomain interactions can induce massive conformational flexibility of DPO4 in favor of anchoring DPO4 to DNA.
source: Our results show that weak interdomain interactions can induce massive conformational flexibility of DPO4 in favor of anchoring DPO4 to DNA (Figure 5, right panel).
evidence: Based on DNA-binding simulation data shown in Figure 4D and Figure 5

claim: The result is reminiscent of the 'fly-casting' effect in the binding process.
source: The result is reminiscent of the 'fly-casting' effect in the binding process (Shoemaker et al., 2000), where the roles of conformational disorder can be appreciated (Huang and Liu, 2009; Levy et al., 2007; Umezawa et al., 2016; Chu and Muñoz, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Shoemaker et al., 2000; Huang and Liu, 2009; Levy et al., 2007; Umezawa et al., 2016; Chu and Muñoz, 2017

claim: The existence of switching from the nonproductive to the productive DPO4–DNA complex has been observed by single-molecule FRET.
source: Experimentally, the existence of switching from the nonproductive to the productive DPO4–DNA complex has also been observed by single-molecule fluorescence resonant energy transfer (FRET) (Brenlla et al., 2014; Raper et al., 2016)
evidence: Supported by citations to Brenlla et al., 2014 and Raper et al., 2016

claim: Switching from the nonproductive to the productive DPO4–DNA complex has been proposed to be essential in completing the DPO4–DNA binding process.
source: and has been proposed to be essential in completing the DPO4–DNA binding process (Raper et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Raper et al., 2018

claim: A decrease in interdomain interaction strength can significantly accelerate the transition from the IS to the BS.
source: Here, we have found that a decrease in interdomain interaction strength can significantly accelerate the transition from the IS to the BS, thus favoring subsequent DNA replication.
evidence: Based on transition time data from Figure 4E

claim: Weak interdomain interactions promote the function of DPO4 as a polymerase for bypassing DNA damage during TLS.
source: Thus, they promote the function of DPO4 as a polymerase for bypassing DNA damage during TLS, which would otherwise stall DNA synthesis in vivo by high-fidelity DNA polymerases (Kunkel and Bebenek, 2000).
evidence: Based on inference from DNA-binding kinetics data and supported by citation to Kunkel and Bebenek, 2000

claim: Very weak interdomain interactions lead to high conformational flexibility in DPO4, resulting in very-low-affinity binding of DNA.
source: Very weak interdomain interactions lead to high conformational flexibility in DPO4 (Figure 4—figure supplement 3), resulting in very-low-affinity binding of DNA, which has been widely observed in IDPs (Wright and Dyson, 1999; Dunker et al., 2001).
evidence: Based on simulation data and supported by citations to Wright and Dyson, 1999 and Dunker et al., 2001

claim: Very strong interdomain interactions quench the conformational dynamics of DPO4, thereby slowing the transitions during the DNA-binding process.
source: On the other hand, very strong interdomain interactions quench the conformational dynamics of DPO4, thereby slowing the transitions during the DNA-binding process and eventually populating the binding complex at the nonproductive IS rather than the productive BS.
evidence: Based on inference from DNA-binding kinetics and conformational distribution data

claim: The default SBM with homogeneously weighted intra- and interdomain interactions can lead to many consistencies in describing the DPO4 folding and DNA–binding processes with experiments.
source: We see that the default SBM with homogeneously weighted intra- and interdomain interactions can lead to many consistencies in describing the DPO4 folding and DNA–binding processes with experiments.
evidence: Based on comparison of simulation results with experimental data

claim: The intermediate state caused by stable individual domain folding during DPO4 folding from the default SBM simulations resonates with the experimentally observed unfolding intermediate.
source: The intermediate state caused by stable individual domain folding during DPO4 folding from the default SBM simulations resonates with the experimentally observed unfolding intermediate (Sherrer et al., 2012).
evidence: Based on comparison of simulation results with experimental data cited from Sherrer et al., 2012

claim: Simulations with the default SBM have described a multistate process for DPO4–DNA binding, in good agreement with the results of previous experiments.
source: In addition, simulations with the default SBM have described a multistate process for DPO4–DNA binding, in good agreement with the results of previous experiments, where the complexity of the processes, including multistep DNA binding and multistate DPO4 conformational dynamics, was revealed (Maxwell et al., 2014; Raper and Suo, 2016; Lee et al., 2017).
evidence: Based on comparison of simulation results with experimental data cited from Maxwell et al., 2014; Raper and Suo, 2016; Lee et al., 2017

claim: The native topologies of DPO4 and the DPO4–DNA complex are major elements in determining the mechanisms of folding and binding, respectively.
source: These features are manifestations that the native topologies of DPO4 and the DPO4–DNA complex are major elements in determining the mechanisms of folding (Clementi et al., 2000) and binding (Levy et al., 2004), respectively.
evidence: Based on inference from simulation results and supported by citations to Clementi et al., 2000 and Levy et al., 2004

claim: DPO4 folding is not the most efficient when the strengths of intra- and interdomain interactions are in the same weights.
source: The SBM simulations with various parameterizations on interdomain interaction strength show that DPO4 folding is not the most efficient when the strengths of intra- and interdomain interactions are in the same weights.
evidence: Based on kinetic simulation data from Figure 3A

claim: The default SBM has led to a significantly enhanced affinity of DPO4–DNA binding and stabilized more on the functionally inactive state IS rather than the functionally active state BS.
source: Furthermore, the default SBM has led to a significantly enhanced affinity of DPO4–DNA binding and stabilized more on the functionally inactive state IS rather than the functionally active state BS, in contradiction with the experiments.
evidence: Based on DNA-binding simulation data from Figure 4A and comparison with experimental data

claim: The weak interdomain interactions in DPO4 are the key to the trade-off between DPO4 folding and function.
source: Considering both the DPO4 folding and the DPO4–DNA binding results, we have suggested that the weak interdomain interactions in DPO4 are the key to the trade-off between DPO4 folding and function.
evidence: Based on synthesis of folding and DNA-binding simulation data

claim: The value of ρ for achieving fast folding and efficient DNA (un)binding appears to be below 1.0.
source: The value of ρ for achieving fast folding and efficient DNA (un)binding appears to be below 1.0.
evidence: Based on synthesis of folding and DNA-binding kinetics data

claim: Within the domains of DPO4, there are a large proportion of conserved hydrophobic residues.
source: This suggestion seems to be reasonable since within the domains of DPO4, there are a large proportion of conserved hydrophobic residues (Ling et al., 2001)
evidence: Supported by citation to Ling et al., 2001

claim: Conserved hydrophobic residues should form stronger interactions inside domains than the ones between domains.
source: which should form stronger interactions inside domains than the ones between domains.
evidence: Based on inference from structural knowledge

claim: DPO4 folds with backtracking, which has been found to be related to the fast and unstable folding followed by the unfolding of the F and T domains.
source: One interesting observation from our simulations is that DPO4 folds with backtracking, which has been found to be related to the fast and unstable folding followed by the unfolding of the F and T domains.
evidence: Based on backtracking analysis from simulation data

claim: The F and T domains in DPO4 are significantly smaller than the corresponding domains in high-fidelity DNA polymerases.
source: Structural analysis has revealed that the F and T domains are significantly smaller than the corresponding domains in high-fidelity DNA polymerases (Ling et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ling et al., 2001

claim: The interactions between the F and T domains and DNA are significantly reduced, providing an explanation of the ability of DPO4 to accommodate and to bypass various DNA lesions.
source: Thus, the interactions between these two domains and DNA are significantly reduced, providing an explanation of the ability of DPO4 to accommodate and to bypass various DNA lesions (Ling et al., 2003; Vaisman et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ling et al., 2003 and Vaisman et al., 2005

claim: Backtracking can help DPO4 to perform TLS by using the structural fluctuations of the domains.
source: Here, we have suggested that backtracking can help DPO4 to perform TLS by using the structural fluctuations of the domains.
evidence: Based on inference from backtracking data and functional considerations

claim: DPO4 binds DNA containing benzo[a]pyrene-deoxyguanosine and allows the bulky lesion to be flipped/looped out of the DNA helix into a structural gap between the F and LF domains.
source: For example, DPO4 binds DNA containing benzo[a]pyrene-deoxyguanosine and allows the bulky lesion to be flipped/looped out of the DNA helix into a structural gap between the F and LF domains (Bauer et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bauer et al., 2007

claim: The structure of DPO4 with DNA containing dG1,8 reveals that the dG moiety of the bulky lesion projects into the cleft between the F and LF domains of DPO4.
source: In addition, the structure of DPO4 with DNA containing 8-(deoxyguanosine-N2-yl)-1-aminopyrene (dG1,8) reveals that the dG moiety of the bulky lesion projects into the cleft between the F and LF domains of DPO4 (Vyas et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Vyas et al., 2015

claim: When ρ is below 1.0 (weak interdomain interactions), the backtracking is not very populated, indicating limited fluctuations in the F and T domains.
source: However, we also note that when ρ is below 1.0 (weak interdomain interactions), the backtracking is not very populated, indicating limited fluctuations in the F and T domains.
evidence: Based on backtracking data from Figure 2—figure supplement 4

claim: Limited fluctuations in the F and T domains may help to maintain the conformational rigidity of the F domain in the DPO4–DNA binding complex, which has been deemed to contribute to the low-fidelity DNA polymerization of DPO4.
source: This may help to maintain the conformational rigidity of the F domain in the DPO4–DNA binding complex, which has been deemed to contribute to the low-fidelity DNA polymerization of DPO4 (Wong et al., 2008).
evidence: Based on inference from backtracking data and supported by citation to Wong et al., 2008

claim: DPO4 may optimize the extent of backtracking represented by the conformational fluctuations in the F and T domains to promote the binding of damaged DNA.
source: Therefore, we speculate that DPO4 may optimize the extent of backtracking represented by the conformational fluctuations in the F and T domains to promote the binding of damaged DNA.
evidence: Based on speculation from backtracking and functional data

claim: DPO4 has naturally evolved to favor simultaneously folding and function.
source: Our results have the important implication that DPO4 has naturally evolved to favor simultaneously folding and function.
evidence: Based on synthesis of all simulation results

claim: The high structural modularity in DPO4 has led to the high thermodynamic modularity that allows an efficient 'divide-and-conquer' mechanism.
source: For folding, the high structural modularity in DPO4 has led to the high thermodynamic modularity that allows an efficient 'divide-and-conquer' mechanism by significantly reducing the number of configurations that need to be searched during folding (Wang et al., 2012a).
evidence: Based on inference from folding data and supported by citation to Wang et al., 2012a

claim: The fastest folding of DPO4 is achieved when the interdomain interactions are weaker than they if they were determined simply by topology.
source: Furthermore, the fastest folding of DPO4 is achieved when the interdomain interactions are weaker than they if they were determined simply by topology.
evidence: Based on kinetic simulation data

claim: The evolutionary pressure has acted on the DPO4 sequence to place more hydrophobic residues inside domains rather than on the domain interfaces.
source: This corresponds to the fact that the evolutionary pressure has acted on the DPO4 sequence to place more hydrophobic residues inside domains rather than on the domain interfaces (Ling et al., 2001).
evidence: Based on inference from simulation results and supported by citation to Ling et al., 2001

claim: Weak interdomain interactions in DPO4 promote functional conformational transition through domain movement and facilitate all transitions throughout the DNA-binding process in favor of DNA replication and lesion bypass.
source: For DNA binding, weak interdomain interactions in DPO4 promote functional conformational transition through domain movement and facilitate all transitions throughout the DNA-binding process in favor of DNA replication and lesion bypass.
evidence: Based on DNA-binding simulation data

claim: The natural evolution of DPO4 requires optimization of its protein sequence to form a structure composed of independently folded domains with hydrophobic cores to handle the folding and DNA-binding processes.
source: Therefore, the natural evolution of DPO4 requires optimization of its protein sequence to form a structure composed of independently folded domains with hydrophobic cores to handle the folding and DNA-binding processes.
evidence: Based on synthesis of all simulation results and evolutionary considerations

claim: All Y-family polymerases share structurally conserved architecture and sequence homology.
source: This expectation is based on the fact that all Y-family polymerases share structurally conserved architecture and sequence homology (Ling et al., 2001; Silvian et al., 2001; Trincao et al., 2001; Uljon et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ling et al., 2001; Silvian et al., 2001; Trincao et al., 2001; Uljon et al., 2004

claim: A large-scale conformational change in the F domains of replicative DNA polymerases upon nucleotide binding is thought to be responsible for their high-fidelity DNA synthesis.
source: A large-scale conformational change in the F domains of replicative DNA polymerases upon nucleotide binding is thought to be responsible for their high-fidelity DNA synthesis (Swan et al., 2009; Johnson, 2010; Prindle et al., 2013; Bębenek and Ziuzia-Graczyk, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Swan et al., 2009; Johnson, 2010; Prindle et al., 2013; Bębenek and Ziuzia-Graczyk, 2018

claim: Such a conformational change is not observed with Y-family DNA polymerases.
source: However, such a change is not observed with Y-family DNA polymerases.
evidence: Based on comparison with replicative DNA polymerases

claim: Differences in topology of multidomain polymerases lead to different folding scenarios and different biological functions.
source: These features imply that differences in topology of multidomain polymerases lead to different folding scenarios and different biological functions.
evidence: Based on inference from structural comparisons
